Then for all integers i,j with 1≤i≤j≤m−1: (i+j<m ⇒ k_i+k_j≥k_{i+j}) and (i+j>m ⇒ k_i+k_j+1≥k_{i+j−m}). No condition is specified for i+j=m.

shared_context.statement_nl: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m, g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m, g) <= N(m, g + 1).

payload.statement_nl: Let S be a subset of N0 = {0,1,2,...} such that 0 belongs to S, S is closed under addition, and N0 \ S is finite; in other words, S is a numerical semigroup. Let m be the least positive element of S, and assume m >= 2. For each integer r with 1 <= r <= m-1, let w_r be the least element of S congruent to r modulo m, and write w_r = r + m k_r with k_r a positive integer. Then the tuple (k_1, ..., k_{m-1}) satisfies the Kunz inequalities: for all integers i and j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let S be a numerical semigroup as in the statement, and let m be its multiplicity, i.e. the least positive element of S, with m >= 2. For each r with 1 <= r <= m-1, let w_r be the least element of S congruent to r modulo m, and write
w_r = r + m k_r.
We first justify that each k_r is a positive integer. Since w_r ≡ r (mod m), the quotient k_r = (w_r-r)/m is an integer. Also w_r cannot equal r, because 1 <= r <= m-1 and m is the least positive element of S, so no positive integer smaller than m belongs to S. Hence w_r > r, so k_r >= 1.

Now fix integers i,j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1.
Because w_i,w_j are in S and S is closed under addition, w_i + w_j belongs to S.
We consider the two cases from the statement.

Case 1: i + j < m.
Then
w_i + w_j = (i + m k_i) + (j + m k_j) = (i+j) + m(k_i+k_j).
So w_i+w_j is an element of S congruent to i+j modulo m. Since 1 <= i+j <= m-1, the residue class i+j is one of the classes for which w_{i+j} is defined, and by definition w_{i+j} is the least element of S congruent to i+j modulo m. Therefore
w_{i+j} <= w_i + w_j.
Substituting the expressions for these numbers gives
(i+j) + m k_{i+j} <= (i+j) + m(k_i+k_j).
Subtract i+j from both sides:
m k_{i+j} <= m(k_i+k_j).
Since m > 0, divide by m to obtain
k_{i+j} <= k_i + k_j,
that is,
k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}.
This is exactly the first Kunz inequality.

Case 2: i + j > m.
Then 1 <= i+j-m <= m-2 < m, so the index i+j-m lies in {1,...,m-1}, and w_{i+j-m} is defined. Again,
w_i + w_j = (i + m k_i) + (j + m k_j) = (i+j-m) + m(k_i+k_j+1).
Hence w_i+w_j is an element of S congruent to i+j-m modulo m. Since w_{i+j-m} is the least element of S in that congruence class, we have
w_{i+j-m} <= w_i + w_j.
Substituting the expressions gives
(i+j-m) + m k_{i+j-m} <= (i+j-m) + m(k_i+k_j+1).
Subtract i+j-m from both sides:
m k_{i+j-m} <= m(k_i+k_j+1).
Since m > 0, divide by m to obtain
k_{i+j-m} <= k_i + k_j + 1,
that is,
k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}.
This is exactly the second Kunz inequality.

Since the two required implications have been proved for every 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, the tuple (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) satisfies the stated Kunz inequalities. This proves the lemma.
result_payload.proof_summary: For each residue class r mod m with 1 <= r <= m-1, the least semigroup element in that class is w_r = r + m k_r with k_r >= 1 because no positive integer < m lies in S. For any i,j, closure of S gives w_i + w_j in S. If i+j < m, then w_i+w_j is congruent to i+j mod m, so minimality of w_{i+j} yields w_{i+j} <= w_i+w_j, hence k_{i+j} <= k_i+k_j. If i+j > m, then w_i+w_j is congruent to i+j-m mod m, so minimality of w_{i+j-m} yields w_{i+j-m} <= w_i+w_j, hence k_{i+j-m} <= k_i+k_j+1.
